  • The official movie poster for Artificial, Luca Guadagnino’s upcoming film about OpenAI, looks like AI slop, only it was drawn by human hands.
  • Industry observers note that anyone who has come across AI-generated images knows they often carry telltale mistakes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that the official movie poster for Artificial, Luca Guadagnino’s upcoming film about OpenAI, looks like AI slop, only it was drawn by human hands. Anyone who has come across AI-generated images knows they often carry telltale mistakes. So when film studio Neon released the poster this week, users on social media were quick to catch oddities in the illustration, leading some to suspect it was made using AI. At first glance, the poster looks normal. On a closer look, Andrew Garfield, who plays Sam Altman in the movie, doesn’t appear quite like himself, lingering somewhere in the uncanny valley. The background features San Francisco’s landscape, except the Golden Gate Bridge is underwater. The tree behind Garfield looks distorted, with a Pinocchio-like face surfacing from the trunk. The branches are no less strange, morphing into snakes. The closer you look, the weirder it gets. Just a few hours after the poster was rolled out on social media, Neon followed up with a video showing a human drawing the scene by hand, crediting illustrator Mike Thompson and creative studio Gravillis. “Art made by humans,” Neon captioned the behind-the-scenes video on X. Art made by humans (Gravillis Inc. and Mike Thompson). https://t.co/0xGxxMKchF pic.twitter.com/XWwBfYU7ym— NEON (@neonrated) November 19, 2026 Users on social media swiftly changed their tune, praising the studio and the movie’s creative team for their approach to the poster design. “The poster for [Artificial] being made by an actual human artist while made to look like it was AI generated wow that’s luca GODagnino,” one user said on X. Another user added, “This poster is a masterpiece. So many fun, completely bizarre, and purposeful ‘AI Slop’ touches. Zoom in and see if you can spot them all.” Many also took notice that Neon didn’t just come out and say the poster was made by humans but rather made the effort to film a behind-the-scenes video and upload it as proof. “Thank you for filming their processes and including the views of the artists in a world where what we see can be compromised or untrue,” one user said on X. People-powered Neon is not the first manufacturer to show how its work was made as a way to stand apart from AI slop. In recent months, brands across retail and tech have done the same. In August, Apple released a behind-the-scenes video of its claymation ad for the new Mac Mini. Prada’s animated holiday campaign includes sketches from the artist. But behind-the-scenes footage works only when the ads themselves are craft-forward, leaning on labor-intensive handwork as a form of effort signaling. While proof of humanness taps into the film’s theme—bringing a sense of irony by making human art look artificial—not every observer is embracing the marketing trend. One X user proclaimed, “Anybody posting any type of art now has to prove to morons that it was genuinely created by them and not AI. What a shit hole time period we live in.”.

The official movie poster for Artificial, Luca Guadagnino’s upcoming film about OpenAI, looks like AI slop, only it was drawn by human hands.

Industry observers note that anyone who has come across AI-generated images knows they often carry telltale mistakes. So when film studio Neon released the poster this week, people on social media were quick to catch oddities in the illustration, leading some to suspect it was made using AI.

At first glance, the poster looks normal.

On a closer look, Andrew Garfield, who plays Sam Altman in the movie, doesn’t appear quite like himself, lingering somewhere in the uncanny valley. The background features San Francisco’s landscape, except the Golden Gate Bridge is underwater. The tree behind Garfield looks distorted, with a Pinocchio-like face surfacing from the trunk. The branches are no less strange, morphing into snakes.

The closer you look, the weirder it gets.

Just a few hours after the poster was rolled out on social media, Neon followed up with a video showing a human drawing the scene by hand, crediting illustrator Mike Thompson and creative studio Gravillis.

“Art made by humans,” Neon captioned the behind-the-scenes video on X.

Recent findings suggest that art made by humans (Gravillis Inc. and Mike Thompson). https://t.co/0xGxxMKchF pic.twitter.com/XWwBfYU7ym.

Users on social media promptly changed their tune, praising the studio and the movie’s creative team for their approach to the poster design.

“The poster for [Artificial] being made by an actual human artist while made to look like it was AI generated wow that’s luca GODagnino,” one user noted on X.

In a recent development, another user added, “This poster is a masterpiece. So many fun, completely bizarre, and purposeful ‘AI Slop’ touches. Zoom in and see if you can spot them all.”.

Many also took notice that Neon didn’t just come out and say the poster was made by humans but rather made the effort to film a behind-the-scenes video and upload it as proof.

“Thank you for filming their processes and including the views of the artists in a world where what we see can be compromised or untrue,” one user stated on X.

Neon is not the first manufacturer to show how its work was made as a way to stand apart from AI slop. In recent months, brands across retail and tech have done the same.

In August, Apple released a behind-the-scenes video of its claymation ad for the new Mac Mini. Prada’s animated holiday campaign includes sketches from the artist.

But behind-the-scenes footage works only when the ads themselves are craft-forward, leaning on labor-intensive handwork as a form of effort signaling.

While proof of humanness taps into the film’s theme—bringing a sense of irony by making human art look artificial—not every observer is embracing the marketing trend.

Industry observers note that one X user proclaimed, “Anybody posting any type of art now has to prove to morons that it was genuinely created by them and not AI. What a shit hole time period we live in.”.

#47035. AI adoption could disproportionately harm Black and Latino workers

AI adoption could disproportionately harm Black and Latino workers

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1118 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that it has become increasingly clear that the AI revolution is not just poised to upend white-collar jobs, despite what public discourse might suggest.
  • It has become increasingly clear that the AI revolution is not just poised to upend white-collar jobs, despite what public discourse might suggest.
  • According to recent reports, the effects of this upheaval will be uneven, which means certain demographic groups are more likely to be impacted.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that it has become increasingly clear that the AI revolution is not just poised to upend white-collar jobs, despite what public discourse might suggest. While entry-level roles are, in fact, on the decline in tech and finance—and employers continue to use AI as a rationale for layoffs—there is ample evidence that rapid AI adoption could interrupt pathways for workers without college degrees. The effects of this upheaval will be uneven, which means certain demographic groups are more likely to be impacted. Some of the jobs that have been deemed “highly exposed” to AI, including clerical and administrative roles, are largely dominated by women, and a newly introduced report from the McKinsey Institute for Economic Mobility posits that Black and Latino workers could also face major consequences. The report finds that Black and Latino workers are overrepresented in the sectors where automation and AI adoption will supplant work altogether, rather than augment work. While the overall rate of AI adoption is relatively stable across different demographics, Black and Latino workers will be affected more acutely by job displacement. Across working hours that are impacted by AI adoption, 40% of hours performed by Black workers and 41% by Latino workers will be displaced (as compared to 37% among white workers). That may not seem like a huge gap. But as the report points out, many of the jobs that are most exposed to AI have historically been pathways to the middle class, making them crucial drivers of social mobility across communities that have faced systemic barriers to entry. Black workers, in particular, dominate six jobs that are likely to see the biggest decline in labor demand, according to McKinsey, including postal mail carriers and customer service representatives; Latino workers are also especially likely to hold some of those jobs, namely dishwashers and hand packers. Black and Latino workers—along with workers in rural regions—are also much more likely to be in jobs that involve physical labor, which are more vulnerable to being automated through robotics and other AI-enabled systems. On the whole, lower-wage workers will face the greatest impact, and are 7.6 times as likely to need to transition into a new job when compared to higher-wage workers; people without a college degree are 1.8 times more likely to need to do the same. Meanwhile, white workers are better positioned to both avoid this level of AI disruption and actually benefit from AI adoption in a number of ways. It’s not just that they’re more likely to hold jobs where AI will enhance their work, boosting productivity rather than replacing employees outright. When compared to their Black and Latino counterparts, white workers are also 30% to 50% more likely to work in the industries where private capital will be deployed, yielding more jobs and wealth creation, the McKinsey report states. That means white workers already have more of a foothold in jobs involving robotics or semiconductors or biotech, setting them up for success as hundreds of billions of dollars pour into those industries. (Look no further than the Anthropic IPO this week, which has created thousands of millionaires.)  In other words: Without broader policy changes or reskilling initiatives, many Black and Latino workers may be forced out of their jobs and locked out of opportunities to cash in on the AI boom.

Tiny flaws in diamonds could unlock a quantum computing revolution

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1172 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A latest computational technique could accelerate the search for diamond materials capable of powering future quantum computers and highly sensitive sensors.
  • It has been revealed that the approach has already revealed newly introduced candidates for quantum computing and sensing applications.
  • One of the biggest challenges in developing quantum technology is finding materials that can maintain delicate quantum states under practical conditions.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A latest computational technique could accelerate the search for diamond materials capable of powering future quantum computers and highly sensitive sensors. Developed by a researcher at the U.S. Department of Energy's (DOE) Princeton Plasma Physics Laboratory (PPPL), the method makes it much easier to identify promising materials for quantum technology, potentially opening the door to advances across many areas of science.

It has been revealed that the approach has already revealed newly introduced candidates for quantum computing and sensing applications. The findings were recently published in ACS Central Science and have attracted attention from other researchers in the field.

One of the biggest challenges in developing quantum technology is finding materials that can maintain delicate quantum states under practical conditions. Many candidates require extremely low temperatures to function reliably. Diamond materials stand out because certain quantum properties can remain useful even at room temperature.

This capability could help advance technologies that are key to national research priorities and the development of next-generation computing. Quantum sensors promise levels of sensitivity and precision beyond those of conventional instruments, while quantum computers could eventually solve certain extraordinarily complex problems much faster than today's most powerful supercomputers.

Why Imperfect Diamonds Could Be the Key to Quantum Computing.

Although diamonds are made of carbon atoms, a flawless diamond crystal is not enough to create a useful quantum computing system. The key lies in tiny irregularities within the crystal structure.

These imperfections, known as defects, can occur when a carbon atom is absent from its normal position, when another element replaces a carbon atom, or when both changes occur together. The atoms surrounding these defects can form qubits, the basic units used to store and process quantum information in quantum computers and sensors.

Finding the most useful defects, however, has been difficult. Accurately modeling their quantum behavior traditionally requires enormous computational resources, making it challenging to evaluate large numbers of possible candidates.

A Simpler Way to Discover Better Diamond Qubits.

Sources indicate that mark Martirez, a staff research scientist at PPPL, developed a way to dramatically reduce the complexity of these calculations. Instead of simulating a much larger diamond structure, he isolates a small region containing just 16 to 30 atoms around a defect.

By "carving out" this tiny atomic cluster and treating it like a separate molecule, Martirez can use powerful computational methods that chemists have spent decades refining. These established techniques make it possible to analyze the quantum properties of diamond defects much more efficiently without sacrificing the high level of accuracy needed for the calculations.

"Because we're treating the qubits as molecules, the cost of calculating these defects is equivalent to the cost of just modeling a simple molecule," Martirez remarked. "This method really opened the floodgates" in terms of how qubits can be assessed.

Sources indicate that the newly introduced technique allows researchers to calculate how different qubits respond to laser light and microwave pulses far more rapidly than before. Using this approach, the team identified promising defects involving boron and oxygen that could serve as new types of qubits.

Fresh Diamond Defects Reveal a Spectrum of Quantum Colors.

Sources indicate that light plays an notable role in how scientists interact with diamond qubits. Researchers use lasers and microwave pulses to manipulate their quantum states and retrieve stored information.

Much of the previous work in this area has centered on a defect known as the nitrogen-vacancy center. This structure forms when a nitrogen atom takes the place of a carbon atom in a diamond crystal, while an adjacent position that would normally contain another carbon atom remains empty.

Under laser illumination, this type of defect can emit red light when it occupies a particular quantum state.

It has been revealed that the newly investigated defects offer different optical properties. Oxygen defects can produce blue light, while those involving boron emit ultraviolet light.

Recent findings suggest that these differences could make it possible to combine several types of qubits within a single quantum device. Because each type responds differently to light, researchers might be able to interact with one group of qubits without disturbing another.

"One could imagine, then, combining different qubits of different responses, so you can basically probe one qubit but not the other," Martirez stated.

Recent findings suggest that beyond identifying newly introduced candidates, the findings suggest a broader change in how researchers approach quantum technology. Diamond qubits have traditionally been studied primarily through physics, but understanding their underlying chemistry could provide additional ways to design them.

Martirez believes that researchers could eventually engineer qubits for particular functions using principles similar to those applied when chemists create specialized molecules, including compounds designed for new medications.

How Quantum Chemistry Could Transform Future Research.

The potential benefits extend well beyond the development of quantum computers themselves. Martirez sees an intriguing possibility in which advances made possible by quantum chemistry eventually lead to quantum technologies that help improve the field of chemistry.

In other words, quantum chemistry could develop the very tools needed to "enrich itself" in the coming decades.

A practical quantum system containing multiple qubits could make molecular calculations substantially more accurate. That would allow scientists to study increasingly complex chemical structures, including large biological molecules and proteins, with a level of detail that is difficult to achieve using conventional methods.

Industry observers note that "We could describe larger molecules, biomolecules, proteins and everything like that in a more accurate way, and that could improve all the chemical-adjacent industries, such as pharmaceutical science and materials science. Even our fundamental understanding of molecular systems could be enriched.".

Such improvements could have far-reaching implications for pharmaceutical development, materials research, and the fundamental study of how molecules behave.

Industry observers note that martirez also hopes the research will encourage more chemists to explore solid-state physics. Although building advanced quantum computers is often viewed as a challenge primarily for physicists, he argues that chemistry offers valuable expertise that could help accelerate progress.

According to recent reports, "At this moment in time, there's a great emphasis on building the first state-of-the-art qubit computer," he said. "But it's not just physicists who should be participating in this research. Chemists have decades of developed intuition about chemical systems that could be easily translated into understanding defects in solids as well.".

By bringing these disciplines together, scientists may be able to develop more effective ways to discover, understand, and eventually engineer the quantum materials needed for future technologies.

The research was funded through PPPL's Laboratory Directed Research and Development program under prime contract number DE-AC02-09CH11466, with additional support from the DOE Office of Science, Office of Fusion Energy Sciences.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Around the office today, you might hear: “May the odds be ever in your favor.” After the tumultuous technical failures of the past week, the phrase might come off as alarming, but it’s actually a Hunger Games reference. The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping hits theaters today and tells Haymitch Abernathy’s origin story. Abernathy is an unlikely hero forced into leadership in the rebellion by circumstances out of his control. This doesn’t mean the C-suite can’t learn a thing or two from him. Here are a few quick stats on the franchise and some of Haymitch’s best management lessons. [Image: Lionsgate] The Hunger Games franchise by the numbers The Hunger Games by Suzanne Collins, the first book in the original trilogy, was published by Scholastic on September 14, 2008. It was followed by Catching Fire in 2009 and Mockingjay in 2010. Before the second book even came out, Lionsgate acquired the film rights for the first book. It was a smart move because the four Hunger Games films have collectively made more than $1.45 billion at the domestic box office. Collins took a break after the first trilogy. A stand-alone prequel novel, The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes, came out in 2020, telling the backstory of Coriolanus Snow. The 2023 film version made more than $166 million at the domestic box office. Sunrise on the Reaping was published in 2025. According to Deadline, the upcoming film is expected to make at least $80 million at the domestic box office on opening weekend alone. Haymitch Abernathy: Reluctant leader archetype Haymitch Abernathy, played by Woody Harrelson in the original films and Joseph Zada in Sunrise, is an unconventional leader. He would rather be drinking away his sorrows than changing the fate of Panem—but sometimes management is thrust upon us. Abernathy excels at strategic planning. In the original books and movies, he is able to guide Peeta and Katniss through the games two times while organizing a rebellion right under the Capitol’s nose. This comes through very careful planning and deception. In the real world, however, business leaders need to be able to communicate a clear vision and how to execute it. Abernathy is rough around the edges—and his tough exterior allows him to work with a diverse range of difficult colleagues to get results. You could call him a people-first strategist. For instance, he was able to get through to Katniss and help her play the public relations game by pretending to have feelings for Peeta. She did that so well that her love for him ended up becoming real. In addition, Abernathy got the vain people of the Capitol to empathize with Katniss and Peeta and send them lifesaving supplies like medicine and water. Initiative, collaborate, and adapt Similarly, managers will have to work with many different personalities, departments, or vendors. True leaders can approach each individual or organization in a way that uplifts their strengths. Back in Panem, all this planning doesn’t mean the reluctant Abernathy can’t adapt. He thrives under pressure. He was the victor of the 50th Hunger Games, the Second Quarter Quell. He had to compete against 47 other tributes, double the usual amount. He won by using the force field around the arena against his opponent. In business, as in the Hunger Games, not everything is going to go according to the five-year-plan. Sometimes you have to improvise solutions as problems arise. As it hits theaters, Sunrise will reveal more of Abernathy’s story and administrative prowess. The business world should take note.

#47029. 4 phases of becoming a great leader

4 phases of becoming a great leader

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3195 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Below, Tony Martignetti shares four key insights from his new book, Illuminating Hidden Brilliance: The Power of Multidimensional Leadership in a One-Dimensional World.
  • Below, Tony Martignetti shares four key insights from his new book, Illuminating Hidden Brilliance: The Power of Multidimensional Leadership in a One-Dimensional World.
  • Recent findings suggest that martignetti is a leadership and workplace culture adviser, global keynote speaker, experience designer, and the host of The Virtual Campfire podcast.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Below, Tony Martignetti shares four key insights from his new book, Illuminating Hidden Brilliance: The Power of Multidimensional Leadership in a One-Dimensional World. Martignetti is a leadership and workplace culture adviser, global keynote speaker, experience designer, and the host of The Virtual Campfire podcast. He began his career as a finance and strategy executive in the high-tech and life sciences industries before leaving the corporate world to help leaders integrate all of who they are into how they lead. What’s the Substantial Idea? The world does not need more exhausted leaders. It needs integrated and multidimensional leaders who can serve as lighthouses for others. If you are ready to stop fragmenting your brilliance and start illuminating it, then the four phases of Illuminating Hidden Brilliance are for you. Listen to the audio version of this Book Bite—read by Martignetti himself—in the Next Big Idea app, or buy the book. 1. Discover The first phase is about uncovering what’s been hidden. For decades, we’ve been sold a seductive story: focus narrowly, pick a lane, master one thing, and leave the rest of yourself at the door. That story made sense in the age of the assembly line, when problems were linear and predictable. That isn’t the world we’re leading in now. I lived this myself. Early in my career, I took pride in being “the numbers guy.” But my real breakthroughs never came from the spreadsheets alone. They came when I paired that analytical rigor with something more creative, like sketching visual maps or drawing metaphors that helped executives feel the strategy instead of just understand it. Now that AI has arrived, it could run those same models in seconds. But it is only able to replace the mechanical part of my contributions. What made me valuable was never the calculations. It was the ability to connect analysis with narrative and logic with imagination. Integration isn’t dilution; it’s differentiation. AI is the ultimate specialist. Our human edge is curiosity, empathy, intuition, creativity, and the ability to make meaning across boundaries. So how do you find what’s been hidden? One way is what I call Flashpoint Excavation. When I began interviewing guests on my podcast, I noticed a pattern. Every leader, whether a CEO, an artist, or a change maker, could trace their most significant growth to a single inflection point: a moment when the old story stopped working and a new one began. Those moments often came disguised as endings. But each one carried an ember of brilliance. When have you hidden a part of yourself to fit the mold of professional success? And what did it cost you? 2. Distill Not every dimension needs equal airtime. Distilling is about deciding what matters most, what wants expression now, and what deserves protection. The heart of this phase is learning to navigate polarities. Being multidimensional means living in constant tension: focus and freedom, logic and intuition, ambition and rest. We’re taught to pick a side and eliminate complexity. But these tensions aren’t flaws to fix. They’re the forces that shape growth. I once coached a healthcare executive who constantly wrestled with the tension between compassion and performance. When we mapped that polarity, she realized her empathy wasn’t softening her results. It was strengthening her influence. Her teams trusted her more deeply, which made accountability easier to sustain. When she stopped choosing between results and relationships, both grew stronger. I think of it like jazz. There’s a structure, a key, a beat, and within it, there’s improvisation. The music works because of the relationship between discipline and play. Leadership works the same way. One of my clients, Alina, keeps a simple note on her desk that reads, “Hold both ambition and humility lightly.” Whenever she feels herself slipping into all-or-nothing thinking, those words bring her back. Distilling also means finding your edge. When I left the corporate world, I thought freedom would be the reward. Instead, I found the chaos of too many possibilities. One morning, after weeks of trying to design the perfect business plan, I closed my laptop, walked outside, and noted to myself, “I don’t need more space. I need better focus.” So, I ran a small experiment. I called it Campfire Conversations: intimate gatherings where leaders shared the stories behind their breakthroughs. That single experiment created a depth I could never have planned, and it became the foundation of my work. I call this the Edge Effect. Brilliance doesn’t happen in endless open space. It happens at the edges, where freedom meets form. 3. Design With clarity in place, the third phase is about designing the practices, rhythms, and environments that sustain your brilliance. This is where leadership becomes intentional instead of reactive. The first quality to design for is elasticity: the capacity to bend without breaking. I love the story of Lego. In the early 2000s, the tech giant was on the verge of collapse. It had expanded into video games, theme parks, fashion, and television. The problem wasn’t too little innovation. It was too much, too fast. When Jørgen Vig Knudstorp became CEO, he did two things that seemed contradictory. First, he set limits. He cut the number of unique pieces in half and guided every decision with one question: Does this build on the brick? Then he opened the doors wider than ever, inviting fans around the world to design new sets. Structure and imagination stopped being enemies and became dance partners. As he put it, “We needed to become smaller and bigger at the same time.” The second piece of Design is Presence Engineering. You cannot live in a multidimensional life with a one-dimensional operating system. Without intentional practices, expressing more of yourself can turn into scattered energy and role-switching fatigue. Presence Engineering gives you a through line that holds your whole identity, so you don’t lose yourself as you expand. When you design for integration, remarkable things can happen. Dina, a cardiac surgeon I once coached, told me privately, “I feel like a robot sometimes.” When I asked her the last time she’d lost herself in the moment, she quietly said, “When I used to paint.” She had hidden that part of herself for years. “You can’t be a serious surgeon and a painter,” she said. A few weeks later, she faced one of the most complex cases of her career. She stepped up to the table and saw the patient’s heart differently. “It looked like something I wanted to paint,” she told me. Her team later described her movement that day as fluid, and almost choreographed, and the surgery was a success. She designed small practices: sketching before difficult cases, taking two minutes outside before scrubbing in, and hanging her paintings in her office. Not only that, but she began telling her residents, “Technical precision saves lives, but your presence saves you.” 4. Deliver The final phase is about extending your integration outward into conversations, teams, organizations, and communities, so your leadership becomes a catalyst for collective brilliance. It often starts with a single conversation. I once worked with a global tech company that was six weeks from a major product launch, and every meeting felt like a battlefield. Engineering said the product wasn’t ready. Marketing said the messaging was unclear. Finance said the budget was already over. No one could see the whole picture. Then a quiet, mid-level product manager stepped in and said, “Before we talk about deliverables, let’s talk about realities. Paint me the picture of what you’re seeing.” Each group sketched its version of the problem on a whiteboard, and as they drew, a pattern appeared that everyone could finally see. Within two days, they’d redesigned the launch, and the product shipped on time. She didn’t solve their problems. What she did was build a bridge between their worlds. That’s the kind of leader the future needs: interpreters and bridge builders who design conversations where people feel seen. To sustain that impact over the long arc of a career, I come back to the image of a lighthouse. A lighthouse doesn’t shine in every direction with equal intensity. It doesn’t react to every wave passing. It stands rooted, and it rotates in a steady rhythm, and its light is focused, which is precisely why ships can steer by it. Think of Ernest Shackleton. In 1915, his ship, the Endurance, was trapped in Antarctic ice and eventually sank. He understood that the greatest danger to his crew was the slow erosion of hope. So he became their lighthouse, moving deliberately between roles: strategist, caretaker, challenger, and anchor, depending on what the moment required. His men later said they watched Shackleton more closely than the sun. Every single crew member survived. His brilliance wasn’t dramatic. It was disciplined. People rarely copy what leaders say. They copy who leaders are. When you model wholeness, you give others permission to bring theirs. The world doesn’t need more exhausted leaders shining endlessly in every direction. It requires integrated, multidimensional leaders who can shine steadily enough to guide others home. You don’t need to become louder, only clearer. And you don’t need to become someone new. You just need to let more of who you already are into the room. This article originally appeared in Next Big Idea Club magazine and is reprinted with permission. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Picking the right earbuds is a tough task, but Samsung’s Galaxy Buds 4 Pro are among the best on the market, and in this guide, we’ll be looking at whether or not they’re the best earbuds for you this holiday season.

This post is sponsored by Samsung.

It has been revealed that in short, yes, the Galaxy Buds 4 Pro sound great. Samsung’s flagship earbuds have a balanced sound profile that’s customizable by the listener to suit their tastes, and is generally recognized as having excellent sound quality by experts and owners alike.

Galaxy Buds 4 Pro are award-winning earbuds with balanced sound quality for music lovers, offering a clean and crisp profile that lets you hear music the way you’ll enjoy it most.

Samsung’s flagship earbuds deliver their sound through a new, larger main driver that’s paired with a dedicated tweeter. They support 24-bit/96 kHz UHQ audio when paired with a compatible Samsung Galaxy device. That’s paired with active noise cancellation that adjust to your surroundings in real-time. They also sound good for those on the other end of a call, with Samsung’s Super Clear Call tech reducing noise from your environment, and the blade stem design positioning the microphones closer to your mouth.

Like everything else in Samsung’s product lineup, Galaxy Buds 4 Pro are packed with useful features.

This includes active noise cancellation (ANC) to filter out noise in your surroundings. Samsung even adapts ANC strength to what’s around you, raising the ANC level when you’re somewhere like on a plane, but lowering it when you’re in a quiet park or café. Voice and Siren Detect can automatically switch the earbuds to Ambient mode when you begin a conversation or when an emergency siren is detected.

Live Translate offers support for 22 languages to help you have a conversation beyond the language barrier, with speech translated into your ears via Buds 4 Pro and the transcript shown on your phone. Bixby and Gemini are accessible through the earbuds for AI assistance, too. Samsung also offers an FDA-approved hearing aid feature to help amplify sounds around you.

In a recent development, head gestures allow you to answer or decline calls with a simple shake of your head. Pinch controls manage playback, while swiping adjusts the volume; pinch-and-hold can be customized for supported shortcuts.

No, you don’t have to have a Samsung Galaxy smartphone to use Galaxy Buds 4 Pro.

Because they work over standard Bluetooth, Samsung’s best earbuds work with any smartphone, tablet, and other devices. Galaxy Buds 4 Pro can also connect to Windows PCs as standard Bluetooth audio, although advanced features are more limited outside the Galaxy ecosystem.

Industry observers note that that noted, you’ll get the best experience with Samsung devices. That’s in part because EQ, noise cancellation, and other controls are baked into One UI, but also because Samsung’s best audio codec on Galaxy Buds 4 Pro is proprietary to Galaxy devices. In other words, you’ll get the best sound quality on these earbuds when paired to another Samsung device.

Galaxy Buds 4 Pro are typically sold for $249.99, but it’s not hard to find a good deal, especially during the holiday season. Best Buy is going to be one of the best resources here, with discounts available throughout the holiday season alongside convenient in-store pickup.

#47026. SNL’s ‘Sister’ sketch hit a nerve, but here’s how to care for elderly parents without upending your life

SNL’s ‘Sister’ sketch hit a nerve, but here’s how to care for elderly parents without upending your life

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3123 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In its 50 years on the air, Saturday Night Live has tackled more than its fair share of social issues.
  • According to recent reports, in its 50 years on the air, Saturday Night Live has tackled more than its fair share of social issues.
  • According to recent reports, this sketch, starring host-for-the-night John Mulaney, promotes Sister™ as the solution to caring for aging parents.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In its 50 years on the air, Saturday Night Live has tackled more than its fair share of social issues. But rarely has an SNL sketch resonated as deeply—and prompted as many national conversations—as the Sister commercial parody that aired on November 14, 2026. This sketch, starring host-for-the-night John Mulaney, promotes Sister™ as the solution to caring for aging parents. The parody claims that simply texting the words “Dad fell” to your sister will prompt her to quit her job, break her lease, and completely upend her life to come take care of him—for free. Clearly, the all-male writing team of Streeter Seidell (who dedicated the sketch to his sister, Heidi), Mikey Day, Simon Rich, and Chase Rosenberg are onto something. AARP found that as of 2025, 59 million Americans were providing care for an adult loved one, and women made up 61% of those caregivers. And it’s taking a toll. AARP reports that caregivers of adults over 50 have been caregiving for 5 years and spend 26 hours per week providing care—up from an average of 3.9 years and 22 hours per week as of 2020. About 20% of those caregivers rate themselves as having fair or poor health, and they report an average of 7 poor mental health days per month. These unpaid caregivers spend an average of $11,508 per year on caretaking, which is equal to 31% of the median household income. Women across the country may have laughed through their rage at this painfully accurate comedy—but they deserve more than the mere satisfaction of simply feeling seen by an incisive satire. Cameron Huddleston, author of Mom and Dad, We Need to Talk, and Dr. Darla Bishop, financial wellness expert, public health researcher, and author of How to Afford Everything, offer the following practical suggestions for how America’s siblings can take care of aging parents without upending their lives, bankrupting themselves, or emptying their retirement accounts. Don’t minimize the costs of caregiving The humor of the SNL sketch relies on the family’s ignoring and downplaying the very real cost the sister pays when she becomes the caregiver. As Dr. Bishop puts it, “If you’re cutting back your hours, turning down promotions, or dipping into your retirement savings, caregiving has a price tag, even when no money changes hands.” But the sister faces more than just financial costs. We see her clash with her father and brother and argue with her husband. “In my work, I teach people to think about their three currencies: time, energy, and money,” Dr. Bishop notes. “Caregiving requires all three.” So rather than the sister being a free resource, as Mulaney claims in the ad, she’s using up all of her currencies while her brother pays nothing. Recognizing the heavy costs of caregiving is the first step to breaking the dynamic illustrated by SNL. “I want families to understand that just because you can afford to help your parents today doesn’t mean you can afford the long-term consequences of doing it alone,” Dr. Bishop says. Don’t ignore available resources “When a parent needs care, families assume they have two choices: do it themselves or pay someone else,” Dr. Bishop says. “But there are resources in between, and finding them could save your family thousands of dollars and countless hours.” Specifically, Dr. Bishop recommends starting with your local Area Agency on Aging, which can help you find services like transportation, meal delivery, respite care, and caregiver support. She also suggests exploring the Eldercare Locator at eldercare.acl.gov to help find affordable caregiving near you. You also don’t have to figure out these services on your own. According to Huddleston, an aging life care professional can help. (These people were previously known as geriatric care managers.) “These professionals will be familiar with resources in your area—from adult day care centers to government programs and community assistance,” Huddleston says. To find an aging life care professional, check out the Aging Life Care Association in your area. And don’t forget other, potentially overlooked resources available to you. Your parents may be eligible for Medicaid, depending on their income, health, and location. The VA’s Aid and Attendance program provides benefits for veterans and their spouses that help cover the cost of assistance with activities of daily living. Even your own employer benefits may help. “Some workplaces offer caregiver support, flexible scheduling, or access to care coordinators,” Dr. Bishop says. Don’t go it alone Huddleston was a caregiver for her mom, who had Alzheimer’s disease. One of her regrets about that time was not asking for more help from her family. “If I had asked, I would’ve gotten more help,” she says, “but I didn’t want to be a burden on others.” This gets to a common mindset the SNL skit illustrates: A lot of women are afraid to ask for help. “We assume it’s our responsibility, and we don’t want to appear like we can’t manage that responsibility,” Huddleston says. While it’s true that sometimes women ask for help and don’t receive it, Huddleston believes that many families assume the caregiver has it covered. “My husband was great about helping with my mom, doing so much to support me and her,” she says. “I’d love to see more men respond that way. But if they’re not seeing the toll it takes on the caregiver, as my husband saw daily with me, they probably aren’t even aware of how much of a sacrifice it is to care for a parent.” When asking for help, Dr. Bishop’s three currencies framework can help you figure out who can do what. You can divide responsibilities based on the time, energy, and money you each bring to the table. “Maybe one sibling lives nearby and can take Mom to appointments while another has more financial flexibility and can contribute toward paid care,” Dr. Bishop suggests. “A third might be great at managing paperwork, coordinating benefits, or researching resources.” Huddleston recommends keeping a running list of the types of support you need so that you’re prepared to make specific requests. “You might ask your brother to find an aging life care professional and cover the cost, to line up a housekeeper or lawn maintenance for your parents’ house, to pay for grocery delivery, to come stay with your parent in the evenings or weekends to give you a break,” she says. She also wants caregivers to let go of any guilt they have about asking for specific help. “It would be easier if men stepped up without being asked to help,” she says. “But if you’re not getting the help you need, don’t feel bad about asking for it.” Don’t wait to make decisions It’s easy to put off thinking about Mom and Dad’s health. None of us like to consider our parents’ mortality, and the idea of losing independence can be terrifying to an aging parent. But it’s easier to make good decisions before Dad falls, when no one is panicked or stressed. That’s why both Huddleston and Dr. Bishop both recommend having a family meeting well before there’s a crisis. “Put everything on the table,” Dr. Bishop says. “Ask yourselves, ‘What does our parent need? What resources do they already have? What can each of us realistically contribute without jeopardizing our own financial security?’” If your family tends to avoid such conversations, Huddleston suggests using the SNL skit as a jumping-off point to start the conversation. Don’t neglect your own long-term care planning Another way to break the cycle of relying on women’s unpaid caregiving is by planning for our own future care needs—and much earlier than you might think. “By the time you’re 50 years old, you should be thinking about long-term care and how you could pay for professional care so that you don’t have to rely entirely on a family member for support,” Huddleston says. “At that age (and into your early 60s if you’re healthy), you can still qualify for long-term care insurance or a hybrid life insurance policy with long-term care benefits.” Dr. Bishop also recommends getting your affairs in order—and that doesn’t just mean having a will in place. “One of the greatest gifts you can give your adult children is not making them play detective during a family crisis,” she says. Specifically, your kids should know where to find your vital documents, who manages your money, what insurance you have, and your wishes in the event that you can’t make medical or financial decisions for yourself. So funny it hurts It’s unlikely that Saturday Night Live expected its three-minute parody to trigger a national reckoning about women’s disproportionate caregiving burden. But it struck a nerve for a very good reason. As Dr. Bishop puts it, “women aren’t the backup plan. We are THE PLAN.” But that doesn’t mean we’re stuck with this dynamic forever. We can end our reliance on women’s unpaid labor by recognizing the heavy time, energy, and money cost of caregiving; exploring all available resources; refusing to let one person handle all caregiving; making proactive decisions; and planning ahead for our own long-term care needs. “The answer isn’t for women to stop caring about their families,” Dr. Bishop says. “It’s for families to stop assuming that caring automatically equals sacrificing your career, your finances, or your own well-being.”.

South Korea busts 54 students cheating on national college admission exam by deploying emergency disaster alert during test

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, south Korea used emergency disaster alerts during its national college admission test to catch prohibited devices.
  • Sources indicate that the College Scholastic Ability Test (CSAT), also known as Suneung, is one of South Korea’s most key yearly events.
  • Industry observers note that the brutal exam, held every third Thursday of November, lasts eight hours, from 8:40 AM to 5:45 PM, often being the deciding factor for the trajectory of the students’ lives.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, south Korea used emergency disaster alerts during its national college admission test to catch prohibited devices. The anti-cheating measure was announced after a cheater in South Korea’s tax accountant exam confessed to using AI and a micro-camera to cheat. The alerts caught a total of 54 candidates, with 111 total when combined with other means, The Korean Herald reports.

Sources indicate that the College Scholastic Ability Test (CSAT), also known as Suneung, is one of South Korea’s most key yearly events. The exam is so significant that the whole country pauses and makes way for the test-takers; police clear the roads and escort late students, noisy construction and maintenance are suspended, aircraft are grounded, military exercises are paused, and the stock market opens an hour later. The government even requests public institutions and private companies start work later, delaying the rush hour and ensuring the students arrive unimpeded.

Industry observers note that the brutal exam, held every third Thursday of November, lasts eight hours, from 8:40 AM to 5:45 PM, often being the deciding factor for the trajectory of the students’ lives. With such high stakes, cheating is not unusual.

In a recent development, the month before the CSAT, South Korea’s Certified Tax Accountant exam received an unusually large number of high scorers — with 66 candidates scoring over 90+ in introductory accounting over only two in 2025 and one in 2024, as reported by The Korean Herald. The top scorer, Han Won-seok, confessed to cheating on his lawyer’s YouTube channel, admitting to cheating using a micro-camera that feeds images of the test to an AI on his smartphone.

The confession went live days before the Suneung, prompting the South Korean government to tighten up its anti-cheating measures for the exam, with Prime Minister Lee Jae Myung stating, "Cheating involving the abuse of AI in South Korea, where public examinations significantly affect the distribution of opportunities and resources, rocks the basic order of our society by undermining fairness and trust," calling for an overhaul of the system to address AI-assisted cheating, as reported by Yonhap News Agency.

Industry observers note that the first alert rang at 8:30 AM, ten minutes before the exam started, catching 31 students with unauthorized devices, whose scores were immediately invalidated despite the test not having started yet. The next two alerts at 2:21 and 2:57 PM caught 23 more, bringing the total to 54. As of today, Yonhap News Agency reports that 111 total students were caught with unauthorized devices — 52 were caught through other methods such as metal detectors, WiFi signal detection, and physical inspections, with a further five caught red-handed using prohibited devices.

According to recent reports, alongside the South Korean government’s reaction to the confession, a law school entrance exam candidate accused of AI-assisted cheating like Han Won-seok had died on the day of the Suneung. In July, Lee Jin-woo, a Legal Education Eligibility Test (LEET) candidate, achieved an impressive perfect score and is reportedly the first to do so. Months later, he published a book about his study methods, talking about lifestyle changes, exercise, diet, and even reduced smartphone use.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

When the tax accountant cheater confessed on Sunday, it led to online suspicion about Lee’s perfect LEET score, with two lawyers even filing legal complaints accusing him of obstruction of official duties. Lee was supposed to be interviewed on YouTube early on Thursday to prove his academic abilities, but he did not show up. Later that day, when Police investigated the legal complaints and after he was reported missing, he was found dead of cardiac arrest at 1:12 PM in a motel, with a note at the scene stating he was mentally and physically exhausted, with no mention of the cheating allegations, as reported by Yonhap News Agency.

While OpenAI helped define the AI boom beginning in late 2021, and Google and other tech giants quickly jumped on the AI train the following year, Apple didn’t make its first real foray into artificial intelligence until 2024 with Apple Intelligence. Though the initial capabilities of Apple Intelligence were rather lackluster compared with its peers, Apple spent the next two years rapidly refining its offerings. In 2026, Apple made its AI system much more capable and expansive by introducing more advanced AI tools, including the Siri AI chatbot and Audio Intelligence. And just last month, Apple also debuted an additional AI tool dubbed “intelligent assistant.” The thing is, Apple now has so many AI offerings that it’s getting hard for the average consumer to keep track of what each one does, which devices support which AI tool, and which tools require a fee to access. So, here’s a cheat sheet for making sense of Apple’s increasingly confusing AI lineup. Apple Intelligence Apple Intelligence is the oldest of the company’s modern AI offerings, introduced in 2024. Think of Apple Intelligence as the foundational artificial intelligence layer integrated into Apple’s operating systems, including iOS, macOS, and watchOS. Apple Intelligence includes a suite of smaller AI tools tailored to specific tasks. For example, Apple Intelligence powers Visual Intelligence, which lets Apple’s AI see and understand what’s on your screen or through your camera and take action on it; for example, it can tell you the nutritional information of the food on your plate. Apple Intelligence powers Audio Intelligence, a tool that can help you identify sounds and music and even recap your spoken conversations on some Apple Watches. It is also the engine behind numerous other AI features across your Apple products, including image generation, live translation, select photo editing tools, message summaries, and more. Not every device that supports Apple Intelligence supports all its features. Any Mac with an Apple Silicon chip will run Apple Intelligence, but you’ll need a Mac with an M3 chip and 12 GB of RAM or more to use some of its most advanced features, including custom Siri Voices and advanced AI dictation. For the iPhone, you’ll need an iPhone 17 Pro or later to use those advanced Apple Intelligence features (iPhone 15 Pro and later is required for most Apple Intelligence features). As for Audio Intelligence on the Apple Watch, that’s limited to the upcoming Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Series 4. Siri AI Siri AI is Apple’s new chatbot. Though people often use the terms “Siri AI” and “Apple Intelligence” interchangeably, they are actually distinct. Apple Intelligence is the foundational AI system integrated into Apple’s operating systems. Siri AI is the natural-language gateway to Apple Intelligence—it lets you communicate as you would with a person to give it commands or find information, which it then carries out using Apple Intelligence’s capabilities. Siri AI runs on the cloud on any device that supports iOS 27, macOS 27, iPadOS 27, visionOS 27, watchOS 27, and (soon) tvOS 27. However, if you want to run some aspects of Siri AI locally on your device, you’ll need a Mac with an M3 chip and 12GB of RAM or more, or an iPhone 17 Pro, iPhone Air, or later. Intelligent Assistant This is Apple’s newest major artificial intelligence tool, the most impressive, and the one that most muddies Apple’s AI branding. “Intelligent assistant,” introduced last month and released this month as part of the updated Logic Pro, Pages, Numbers, and Keynote apps in Apple’s paid Creator Studio suite, is a new natural-language AI tool aimed at helping creators be more productive. The tool is integrated into the above apps in the form of a chatbot. There’s a text field where you type instructions to the intelligent assistant (“make this piano track sound like it was recorded in a concert hall” or “fix the formula errors in this spreadsheet”). The changes happen like magic—all very impressive stuff. As a matter of fact, it’s way more impressive than the other capabilities Apple has shown off for Apple Intelligence and Siri AI. So why hasn’t Apple branded these new AI features as Apple Intelligence? The answer: Intelligent assistant is not powered by Apple Intelligence or Siri AI. Instead, the new AI tools use Apple Foundation Models combined with additional models from third-party providers, in this case, OpenAI and Google. This explains why intelligent assistant is so capable (both OpenAI and Google have a huge lead over Apple in the AI space) and also why Apple has eschewed the Apple Intelligence branding for the work it carries out. Does Apple charge for AI? This is where things get really muddied for people. Apple’s AI pricing runs from free, to a monthly subscription fee, to higher usage limits with select iCloud Plus plans. Presently, using Apple Intelligence and Siri AI is free for all people. However, Apple says this won’t last. With the release of the 27.3 versions of its operating systems in December, customers will have daily limits when using Siri AI and Apple Intelligence. If they exceed those limits, they won’t be able to use any Apple Intelligence features that require cloud processing (which costs Apple compute power). If users do want higher Apple Intelligence and Siri AI limits, they can get more by paying for an iCloud Plus blueprint (if they don’t already have one). The 50GB iCloud Plus plan, which costs just 99 cents per month, doesn’t increase your AI limits. However, the other iCloud Plus plans do: 200GB ($2.99 per month): 2x limit increase 2TB ($9.99 per month): 5x limit increase 6TB ($29.99 per month): 10x limit increase 12TB ($59.99 per month): 20x limit increase As for intelligent assistant access in Logic Pro, Pages, Keynote, and Numbers, users already need to pony up. Intelligent assistant is available only as part of Apple’s Creator Studio subscription bundle, for which it charges $12.99 per month or $129 per year. This means that if you want as much access as possible to Apple’s AI offerings, you’ll need to subscribe to two subscription plans.

Housing market shift: 76 metros where home prices are falling

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that want more housing market stories from Lance Lambert’s ResiClub in your inbox?
  • Want more housing market stories from Lance Lambert’s ResiClub in your inbox?
  • Sources indicate that based on ResiClub’s analysis of the Zillow Home Value Index, nationally aggregated U.S.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that want more housing market stories from Lance Lambert’s ResiClub in your inbox? Subscribe to the ResiClub newsletter. Based on ResiClub’s analysis of the Zillow Home Value Index, nationally aggregated U.S. home prices rose 0.7% year over year from October 2025 to October 2026. That marks another month-over-month deceleration, down from the 1.0% year-over-year increase from September 2025 to September 2026 and the 1.3% year-over-year increase from August 2025 to August 2026. After contracting over the past year, the number of America’s major regional housing markets seeing year-over-year declines is rising again, as the already soft national housing market (which is still amid the multiyear post-boom cyclical cooling window) sees another burst of softening amid the recent run-up in long-term yields and mortgage rates. —> 54 of the nation’s 300 largest housing markets (i.e., 18% of markets) had a falling year-over-year home price reading in the August 2025 to August 2026 window. —> 66 of the nation’s 300 largest housing markets (i.e., 22% of markets) had a falling year-over-year home price reading in the September 2025 to September 2026 window. —> 76 of the nation’s 300 largest housing markets (i.e., 25% of markets) had a falling year-over-year home price reading in the October 2025 to October 2026 window. We should point out that the nationally aggregated housing market is softer than the counts above suggest, given that year-over-year home price declines are currently skewed slightly toward larger metro areas. Home prices are still climbing a tad nominally (not inflation-adjusted) year over year in some pockets where active inventory remains well below pre-pandemic 2019 levels, such as certain areas in the Northeast and Midwest. In contrast, some pockets in states like Texas, Florida, Washington, and Colorado—where active inventory exceeds pre-pandemic 2019 levels by a solid clip—are seeing either material corrections, modest home price pullbacks, or simply flat pricing. Looking ahead, the big question is how much of a burst of softening the nationally aggregated housing market will see, now that the 30-year fixed-mortgage rate has jumped back above 7.0% amid an already strained affordability environment and the still ongoing post-boom cyclical cooling period. To keep an eye on it, ResiClub recommends closely monitoring local active inventory/months of supply over the next several months. Click here for an interactive version of the chart below. Many of the housing markets seeing the most softness, where homebuyers have gained the most leverage since the pandemic housing boom fizzled out, are primarily located in Sunbelt regions or the Mountain West. Many of these areas saw even greater price surges during the pandemic housing boom, with home price growth outpacing local income levels. As pandemic-driven domestic migration slowed and mortgage rates rose in 2022, markets like Tampa, Florida, and Austin faced challenges, relying on local income levels to support frothy home prices. That Sunbelt softening was further compounded by an abundance of upcoming-home supply in the Sunbelt. Builders are often willing to lower prices or offer affordability incentives to maintain sales, which also has a cooling effect on the resale market. As a result, some buyers who might have previously opted for existing homes are instead choosing new construction with more attractive deals—which added further upward pressure to resale inventory growth over the past few years. Of course, while 76 of the nation’s 300 largest metro-area housing markets are seeing year-over-year home price declines, another 224 are seeing year-over-year home price increases. However, most of the places posting “nominal gains” are seeing gains below income growth and consumer price growth, which economists call “real” (inflation-adjusted) home price declines. Where are home prices still up on a year-over-year basis? See the map below. Below is a historical chart showing the year-over-year change in home prices across the 50 largest metro housing markets, with the yellow line representing the national aggregate, dating back to 2000. While the range [see chart above] between the strongest and weakest metro-area housing markets right now is fairly normal historically speaking, the bifurcation (i.e., direction) itself—the share of markets with rising home prices versus those with falling prices—is wider than normal, given that national appreciation is in a softer market with growth barely above 0.0%. And the longer some markets remain in the “rising” camp while others stay in the “falling” camp, the wider the gulf can become between the relatively more resilient markets and the weaker ones. For example, home prices in the Hartford, Conneticut, metro area are now 28.0% above their 2022 peak, while home prices in the Austin metro area sit 28.8% below their 2022 peak. Some of that bifurcation boils down to mean reversion, with many of the outright home price declines occurring in markets that overheated further during the pandemic housing boom. Note: For the historical chart below, we analyzed the 200 largest markets rather than the 300 used above, as some markets ranked 201 to 300 lack complete data going back to 2000. When weighted by population (not visualized), the housing market appears slightly weaker than the chart below suggests—which aligns with the fact that among just the 50 largest housing markets, 21 (42%) are currently posting negative year-over-year price growth, and nationally aggregated home prices are up just 0.7% year over year using the Zillow Home Value Index.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Motorola’s upcoming Razr Flex foldable is expected to have the same wide foldable form factor as Galaxy Z Fold 8 and iPhone Duo, and upcoming leaks not only reveal its design, but hint at some key specs.

Sources indicate that ahead of its supposed 2027 debut, the Motorola Razr Flex has now leaked in a real-life image. The image demonstrates the back of the phone with a dual-camera setup, Pixel-like camera bar, and a design that matches that short and stout look of Galaxy Z Fold 8 and iPhone Duo. It also pretty clearly lines up with past teasers of this device.

Rumor has it that the Razr Flex will be even smaller than Samsung or Apple’s wide foldables, and the proportions of this image make that all the more certain.

Beyond this, some regulatory leaks reveal key specs on the Motorola Razr Flex.

The foldable will apparently run Android 17 out of the box – an revision that Razr Fold is only getting just now – and run on the Qualcomm SM8845 Pro chipset. Android Authority notes that this isn’t a chip that’s been announced yet, but it’s thought to be called “Snapdragon 8 Gen 5 Pro.”.

Other rumored specs include a 4.97-inch outer display, 6.92-inch inner display, 5,000 mAh battery, 12GB of RAM, and two 50MP cameras around back. Based on information from a past leak, the color variant pictured above is likely called “Coriander.”.

#47020. Canva added an AI ‘kill switch’ to its tools

Canva added an AI ‘kill switch’ to its tools

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1496 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that over the last few years, Canva, the Australian design platform, has been stuffing generative AI into its products.
  • Over the last few years, Canva, the Australian design platform, has been stuffing generative AI into its products.
  • The first button seems like pure theater to me.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that over the last few years, Canva, the Australian design platform, has been stuffing generative AI into its products. Now, it’s giving you the option to make those AI features disappear. On Thursday, the company announced two latest switches to rein in its AI for anyone on Canva Free and Canva Pro. One toggle button hides its generative AI features. Another one will make Canva show less AI-generated material in its library of templates and graphics. The first button seems like pure theater to me. If a user doesn’t want to use AI tools, it’s easy enough to figure out how: Don’t press the sparkly AI button. The second one is more useful, however, since it can help consumers avoid being drowned by AI-generated material while browsing the Canva libraries that made this suite popular in the first place. It’s worth noting that the switch doesn’t ban all AI-generated material from view—it just demonstrates less. [Image: Canva] Both switches are buried in two settings menus. The general AI “kill switch” lives under Profile > Settings > Permissions. Flip it off, and Canva’s generative features are “hidden across Canva,” the company said in an announcement. These include Magic Expand, which extends a photo, and Canva Craft, the first generative image model developed by the company. You can turn them back on whenever you like. Still, Canva hasn’t erased every AI thingamajig. The suite’s AI-based Background Remover and Magic Grab—which picks an object out of a picture to move it somewhere else in the design—are “assistive editing tools,” and therefore are still accessed after toggling AI off. The second control sits under Profile > Your Account > AI Personalization (more on this later). Turn it on, and Canva cuts back the AI-generated material that pops up in search results and recommendations, pushing more human-made stuff to the top. The company claims its AI content is only “a small portion” of its library, like abstract backgrounds and illustrated graphics. [Image: Canva] Why, really The filter matters to people who don’t want to wade through a river full of generative AI creations. It also benefits the humans behind the designs. Canva pays actual humans each time someone uses their work in a design. In theory, that steers money toward the designers and illustrators who fill the Canva library. These features are essentially a temperature check on AI. Canva tied the launch to the public mood, citing Pew Research Center figures: Roughly 6 in 10 Americans say they want more control over how artificial intelligence is used in their lives. “We believe the future of creativity should be defined by choice, not dictated by technology,” the company said in a statement. In an email, Canva says it is “always listening to our community and looking for ways to make Canva work better for them. We’ve heard that people want more choice over AI, and these controls are one way we’re responding. . . . These controls give people more choice over how AI fits into their Canva experience.” But if Canva really wanted to make this happen, why bury the controls? If you want to empower your users and creators, there’s no reason to hide the settings. Rather, you should add the switches right there on the main interface so that people can choose their experience with ease. The company says that putting clearly visible AI kill switches right on the main interface, for every user to see right away, is something they are “actually exploring.” Perhaps Canva fears that too many people will choose to deactivate these features, cutting off one of its revenue streams. After all, in the same announcement, Canva said that its community has used its AI tools more than 38 billion times. The company also says it’s still investing to make its AI wares “even more powerful.” And remember: Canva just built its own generative image model to help shave the costs of so many people using its AI tools. AI is still very much a priority for the company. Canva claims that “this isn’t a marketing play” and that it is just a temporary solution: “Our goal was to get a solution live to our community as rapidly as possible, but that doesn’t mean this is its final form. While it’s early, the response is telling us that people are excited to have this option, but we’ll listen for signals on how it should evolve.”.

It’s worth noting that the switch doesn’t ban all AI-generated material from view—it just demonstrates less.

Recent findings suggest that both switches are buried in two settings menus. The general AI “kill switch” lives under Profile > Settings > Permissions. Flip it off, and Canva’s generative features are “hidden across Canva,” the company said in an announcement. These include Magic Expand, which extends a photo, and Canva Craft, the first generative image model developed by the company. You can turn them back on whenever you like.

It has been revealed that still, Canva hasn’t erased every AI thingamajig. The suite’s AI-based Background Remover and Magic Grab—which picks an object out of a picture to move it somewhere else in the design—are “assistive editing tools,” and therefore are still accessed after toggling AI off.

Sources indicate that the second control sits under Profile > Your Account > AI Personalization (more on this later). Turn it on, and Canva cuts back the AI-generated material that pops up in search results and recommendations, pushing more human-made stuff to the top. The manufacturer notes its AI content is only “a small portion” of its library, like abstract backgrounds and illustrated graphics.

The filter matters to people who don’t want to wade through a river full of generative AI creations. It also benefits the humans behind the designs. Canva pays actual humans each time someone uses their work in a design. In theory, that steers money toward the designers and illustrators who fill the Canva library.

These features are essentially a temperature check on AI. Canva tied the launch to the public mood, citing Pew Research Center figures: Roughly 6 in 10 Americans say they want more control over how artificial intelligence is used in their lives. “We believe the future of creativity should be defined by choice, not dictated by technology,” the company said in a statement.

In an email, Canva notes it is “always listening to our community and looking for ways to make Canva work better for them. We’ve heard that people want more choice over AI, and these controls are one way we’re responding. . . . These controls give people more choice over how AI fits into their Canva experience.”.

Sources indicate that but if Canva really wanted to make this happen, why bury the controls? If you want to empower your consumers and creators, there’s no reason to hide the settings. Rather, you should add the switches right there on the main interface so that people can choose their experience with ease. The firm notes that putting clearly visible AI kill switches right on the main interface, for every user to see right away, is something they are “actually exploring.”.

According to recent reports, perhaps Canva fears that too many people will choose to deactivate these features, cutting off one of its revenue streams. After all, in the same announcement, Canva said that its community has used its AI tools more than 38 billion times. The manufacturer also indicates it’s still investing to make its AI wares “even more powerful.” And remember: Canva just built its own generative image model to help shave the costs of so many people using its AI tools. AI is still very much a priority for the company.

It has been revealed that canva claims that “this isn’t a marketing play” and that it is just a temporary solution: “Our goal was to get a solution live to our community as quickly as possible, but that doesn’t mean this is its final form. While it’s early, the response is telling us that people are excited to have this option, but we’ll listen for signals on how it should evolve.”.

Latest Update: Players are coming to ‘GTA VI’ for the car chases, but staying for the wildlife

💡 Key Takeaways
  • After a 13-year wait, Rockstar Games’s Grand Theft Auto VI has been released—but for many players, a life of crime isn’t the only appeal.
  • After a 13-year wait, Rockstar Games’s Grand Theft Auto VI has been released—but for many players, a life of crime isn’t the only appeal.
  • The game is set in Leonida (Florida, but fictionalized), and outside Vice City’s limits, the state’s characteristic swamps, waters, and subtropical forests sprawl across the map.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

After a 13-year wait, Rockstar Games’s Grand Theft Auto VI has been released—but for many players, a life of crime isn’t the only appeal. The game is set in Leonida (Florida, but fictionalized), and outside Vice City’s limits, the state’s characteristic swamps, waters, and subtropical forests sprawl across the map. Expansive, painstakingly rendered landscapes have long been an integral part of Rockstar’s open-world action-adventure games, including its last major release, Red Dead Redemption 2. As in that title, in GTA VI, the natural world is more than just a backdrop for the main story: Side quests like alligator hunting and a zoologist challenge lead players into the great outdoors. Players have eagerly anticipated the wildlife. A promotional image featuring a lionfish—an invasive species in Florida—sparked hopeful discussion about spear hunting, which is one of the methods used to control their population. Other fans kept running lists of species confirmed ahead of the release date. GTA VI’s birding gameplay and inclusion of 62 avian species has been a particular source of buzz online, and hobbyists are already logging the species they spy on a dedicated website called Leonida Birds. One person said that playing Red Dead Redemption 2 had “flipped the birding switch on,” and that they’ve since identified birds from the game in real life. Perhaps unsurprisingly, research suggests that this deep immersion in video game environments can serve as a valuable way to communicate information about the real natural world, including a study in which RDR2 players correctly identified more photos of wildlife species that had appeared in the game than non-players. “Not sure how GTA VI has suddenly turned me into David Attenborough,” one player remarked on X, “but I just logged off an 8 hour session and immediately want to hop back on to study more birds and wildlife.” In a study published in Geoscience Communication this week, researchers used GTA V’s digital replication of Los Angeles—coupled with data like Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change projections and records of past flooding—to simulate floods caused by sea level rise. Paul Nörenberg, one of the researchers, said in a press release that engaging with these climate effects in a familiar landscape “can bridge a gap in a way that conventional visualizations, such as models or maps, struggle to achieve.” Another study, which interviewed gamers about their experiences, observed that different games allow participants to explore nature through different contexts and perspectives, and games that include environmental destruction “made them contend with exploiting and subjugating nature—both in-game and in the actual world.” Though Grand Theft Auto’s plots are designed to let players explore a life of crime—not climate disaster—the upcoming installment’s gameplay does weave in a range of real-world environmental topics, from animal conservation to chemicals in agriculture. One mission centers on the exotic animal trade; another involves freeing an orca from the Vice City Oceanarium, likely a reference to the now-shuttered Miami Seaquarium, which faced criticism for owning an orca named Lolita that died in captivity in 2023. In a third, a strawberry grower asks the player to visit a meth lab to pick up “discontinued” chemicals that he sprays on his unnaturally large crops, according to an IGN walk-through. This also echoes reality. Driscoll’s, a major agribusiness, faces a class-action lawsuit that alleges the manufacturer sold strawberries contaminated with harmful chemicals without disclosing them. Video game realism does have its limits: The real-life strawberries haven’t turned anyone into giant mutants. Yet.

Recent findings suggest that expansive, painstakingly rendered landscapes have long been an integral part of Rockstar’s open-world action-adventure games, including its last major release, Red Dead Redemption 2. Players have eagerly anticipated the wildlife. One person noted that playing Red Dead Redemption 2 had “flipped the birding switch on,” and that they’ve since identified birds from the game in real life.

Perhaps unsurprisingly, research suggests that this deep immersion in video game environments can serve as a valuable way to communicate information about the real natural world, including a study in which RDR2 players correctly identified more photos of wildlife species that had appeared in the game than non-players.
